title: Scaffold archive-api and prove the Identity Map
description: Set up a local Postgres database named 'archive'. Install @mikro-orm/core, @mikro-orm/postgresql, and @mikro-orm/reflection. Create mikro-orm.config.ts pointing at that database. Define a Book entity with id (bigint PK), title (string, max 200), and createdAt (datetime). Write main.ts that: (1) calls MikroORM.init(), (2) persists two Book instances in one flush, (3) fetches one of them by id, and (4) console.log('same instance?', book === fetched). Run npm start and capture a screenshot of your terminal showing the INSERT log, the SELECT log, and 'same instance? true' on the same screen.
modelAnswer:
The terminal should show:
1. A BEGIN statement followed by batched INSERTs (both books in one transaction), then COMMIT.
2. A single SELECT WHERE id = <n> for the findOne call.
3. 'same instance? true' — confirming the Identity Map returned the already-managed object instead of constructing a new one.
If you see two SELECTs, the entity was not registered before the second findOne — check that you called em.persist() before em.flush(), not em.insert().

title: Explain the Unit of Work in your own words
description: In 4–6 sentences answer: what does the Unit of Work pattern do, and why does MikroORM flush all changes in a single transaction rather than one-by-one? Use at least one concrete example tied to the Records Library analogy (the librarian, the catalogue card, the reading room). Submit as text.
modelAnswer:
A good answer covers three things:
1. The Unit of Work collects every change made to managed entities during the request (new, modified, removed) without touching the database yet.
2. On flush(), MikroORM orders those changes by foreign-key dependency and wraps them in a single transaction — so either everything lands or nothing does.
3. Library analogy: the librarian takes notes on every change you make at the reading-room desk (new catalogue cards, corrections, withdrawals), then at closing time walks to the storeroom once and commits everything in the right order — not once per correction.
Watch for: answers that conflate the Identity Map with the Unit of Work. They cooperate, but the Identity Map is about uniqueness of instances; the UoW is about deferred write batching.

title: Why is the Identity Map per-request, not global? (AI-resilient)
description:
Draft a 3–5 sentence answer explaining why a shared, global Identity Map would be catastrophic in a multi-request web server. Then test your answer: paste your draft into ChatGPT and ask it to improve it. Identify one thing ChatGPT added or changed that you agree with, and one thing it missed or got wrong. Submit: your original draft, the ChatGPT output, and your one-line verdict on each. (Hint: think about concurrent requests mutating the same in-memory Book instance, and what 'stale data' means when 50 HTTP handlers share one map.)

Metacognitive memo: What was hard to articulate? What would an AI summary of this lesson probably miss about why per-request isolation matters?
modelAnswer:
Key reasoning the answer must include:
1. Two concurrent requests could load the same entity id into the same JS object. Request A mutates it; flush from Request B now writes Request A's dirty data to the database under Request B's transaction — silent data corruption.
2. A global map never gets cleared: entities loaded six hours ago stay 'managed', occupying memory and presenting stale state to any handler that asks for them.
3. Per-request fork() gives each handler its own reading-room; the head librarian's master catalogue is the source of truth, but each patron's desk is private.
AI limitation: ChatGPT typically gives a technically correct but surface-level answer. It often misses the flush-ordering issue under concurrent mutations — that it is not just a memory leak but a correctness bug.

title: Why does MikroORM choose Data Mapper over Active Record?
description: Why does keeping persistence logic out of the entity class make the domain model easier to test, and why doesn't that benefit show up on small projects? Answer in 4–6 sentences. Consider: what does an Active Record entity need to import to call .save(), and what does that import do to your unit tests?
modelAnswer:
Core reasoning:
1. An Active Record entity must import a DB adapter or connection pool. Unit tests therefore need a real (or mocked) database connection just to instantiate the model — the test suite becomes an integration test suite by default.
2. With Data Mapper, the entity is a plain class with no DB imports. You can new Book({ title: '...' }) in a unit test without touching Postgres at all.
3. The benefit is invisible on small projects because the entire app may already be one integration test or no tests at all. The cost of the Active Record coupling only shows up when you want to test business rules in isolation — which at Fohlio means testing a pricing rule without spinning up a database.
4. The trade-off is indirection: you need to learn EntityManager, whereas Active Record's user.save() is immediately obvious to a junior.
